activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
knowledge_domain: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
fact: A new baby cannot talk yet, so it cries to show it needs something.
story:
Henry went to the hospital with Dad. Mom was holding a new baby. "This is your baby sister," said Mom. She was very young and very small.

The baby began to cry. Henry put his truck down. The truck had sand in it from the yard at home. "Why is she crying?" Henry asked.

"She cannot talk yet," said Mom. "She cries to show she needs something."

"Maybe she needs milk," said Henry. Mom gave the baby some milk. The baby drank. Then she stopped crying. Henry clapped his hands.

The baby cried again. "Maybe she needs a hug," said Henry. Mom held her close. The crying stopped again.

Henry leaned over very slowly. He gave the baby a kiss on her head. The baby looked at him. "I will listen to you," said Henry. "Every day."

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
knowledge_domain: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
fact: A steady beat stays even and keeps going, like footsteps when you march.
story:
Gabriella sat on a small red chair at Miss Penny's music studio. Miss Penny put on a song. "Clap with me," she said. Gabriella clapped. But her claps went fast, fast, fast. Then they stopped. The song kept going without her.

Gabriella frowned. "My claps ran away," she said. Miss Penny smiled. "Try marching," she said. Gabriella stood up. She marched around the room. Stomp, stomp, stomp. Her feet went even, like walking down the hall. The song kept going too. Her feet and the song went together.

"Can you clap like your feet?" asked Miss Penny. Gabriella clapped. Clap, clap, clap. Steady and even. Then she sang, "Baa, baa, black sheep, have you any wool?" She did not stop. She clapped and sang all the way to the end. Miss Penny clapped too. "Again!" said Gabriella.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Seeds need water to start growing.
story:
Jordan planted seeds in the school garden. He made a deep little hole for each one. Then he patted the soil on top. "Grow, little seeds," he said.

Every morning Jordan ran to the garden. He saw a carrot patch. Maya's seeds had green shoots. Ben's seeds had green shoots. Jordan's pot had nothing at all. Just brown dirt. Jordan sat down in the circle of friends. He did not want to share his sad face.

Then he saw Maya hold her watering can. She tipped it over her shoots. Drip, drip, drip. Jordan touched his soil. It was dry and crumbly. He had never given his seeds any water. Jordan found his own little can. He filled it at the tap. He poured the water slowly and softly over the dirt.

The next morning, Jordan tiptoed to the pot. A tiny green shoot was peeking out. It had a little white hat of seed shell on top. Jordan clapped his hands. "Hello, little plant!" he called. Maya peeked over and smiled. "Mine did that too," she said. Jordan held up his watering can with both hands. "Water time," he said.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: The counting words always go in the same order: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten.
story:
Ivy ran to the swings on a warm summer day. A little boy stood by the sandbox, counting his trucks. "One, two, four," he said. His face looked sad.

His big sister knelt down beside him. "You missed three," she said. "It goes one, two, three, four."

Ivy watched. The boy tried again. "One, two, three, four," he said. Now he smiled big. "More trucks!" said his sister. He counted on. "Five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

Ivy wanted to count too. She found ten little stones by the slide. She tapped each stone with one finger. "One, two, three," she said. She stopped. What came next? She thought hard. Then she heard the boy singing behind her. "One, two, three, four!"

"Four!" said Ivy. She tapped the next stone. Careful, she told herself, so the stones would not spill out of her hand. "Five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten stones, all counted.

The boy ran over. "You said them all!" he said.

"Want to count my stones?" asked Ivy. She poured them into his hands. "One, two, three," they sang together, all the way to ten.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
fact: Sunscreen helps protect your skin from sunburn.
story:
Jasmine ran to the door. "Park day!" she called. Her mom held up a bottle. "Wait, Jasmine. Sunscreen first." Jasmine stamped her foot. "Why?" she asked. "The sun is so shiny and bright," said Mom. "Sunscreen helps protect your skin." Mom rubbed it on Jasmine's arms. She rubbed it on Jasmine's neck. "Now we can go."

The park was hot and sunny. Jasmine played on the swings. The wind blew her hair. The wind blew the leaves. Big clouds came. Drip, drip, drop. Rain fell! Mom opened an umbrella. Then the rain turned soft and white. "Snow in summer?" asked Jasmine. "No," said Mom. "It is just petals from the tree."

Jasmine picked up a petal. She put it in her pocket to take home. Her friend Ben sat on the bench. His face was red. "I forgot my sunscreen," he said. Jasmine looked at her arms. They were not red. "Come on," she said. "My mom has more. She can rub some on you." Ben smiled and took her hand.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
fact: Birds are animals that have feathers.
story:
Hazel set her toys on the grass. She lined up her bear, her ball and her truck. Then she put out pretend food. There was a play apple, a play banana and a play cake. "Time to eat!" she said.

A soft sound came from the fence. Peck, peck, peck. A little brown bird was there. Hazel held out her hand very still. The bird flew down. It took a crumb of play cake and flew away.

Then Hazel saw something on the grass. It was small and gray and straight along one edge. "A feather!" she said. She ran to Mom. "A bird lost this. Birds are animals that have feathers." Mom nodded and smiled.

Hazel put the feather in her pocket. At bedtime it stayed under her pillow, straight and soft, waiting for morning.

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
knowledge_domain: learning to swim at the local pool
fact: A lifeguard's job is to watch the swimmers and help anyone who needs it.
story: Leah stood in the pool changing room. She pulled on her little swimsuit. Her swim lesson started soon. "Why does the lifeguard sit up so high?" she asked Mama. "I wonder too," said Mama. "Let's go watch." They walked out to the pool. The lifeguard sat in a tall chair. Leah looked up, up, up. From up there, the lifeguard could see every swimmer in the pool. Then a boy splashed too far. He could not touch the bottom. His arm went up. The lifeguard blew the whistle. She jumped down fast. She helped the boy back to the wall. He held on and smiled. Leah's eyes went wide. "She was watching him the whole time," Leah whispered. After her lesson, Leah waved at the tall chair. The lifeguard waved back. "I saw you swim," she called down. Leah grinned all the way to the changing room.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
fact: Writing your name on a toy's tag helps people know it belongs to you.
story:
Mason lost his monkey. His soft, spotted monkey was gone. He looked at Grandma's house. He looked under the bed. No monkey. He looked in the big chair. No monkey. He looked in the toy box. No monkey.

"Where can he be?" Mason asked. Grandma said, "Did you take him outside?" Mason had played by the gate. He ran to look. There was his monkey, sitting by the fence! But then a bus stopped. A kind driver held up the monkey. "Who lost this?" she asked. She looked at the tag. It said Mason. "This tag has your name," she said. "Now I know he is yours."

Grandma helped Mason write his name on the tag. Mason read it out loud. "M, A, S, O, N." His name was on his monkey. Grandma said, "Now everyone will know." Mason hugged his monkey tight. "Home with me," he whispered.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Soon means in a little while.
story:
Athena went to the store with Grandma. Yesterday they had no milk at home. Today they needed to buy some. Athena held Grandma's hand in the big store.

Athena saw a pink balloon by the door. It floated up high. "Can I have one?" she asked. "Soon," said Grandma. "First we get the milk." Athena made a sad face. Soon felt like a long, long time.

They walked past the bread. They walked past the apples. Athena helped put the milk in the cart. Then they found cheese. The cart got full. It was not full yesterday. It was full now.

Then Grandma stopped walking. She pointed at the balloons. "Now," she said. Athena picked a pink one. She did not have to wait forever. Soon was just a little while.

At the bus stop, Athena held her balloon tight. The bus came down the street. "Today was a good day," said Grandma. Athena smiled. "Tomorrow can we come back?" she asked. Grandma laughed and hugged her. The bus doors opened with a big whoosh, and Athena stepped up, holding her pink string high.

activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
knowledge_domain: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
fact: The alphabet starts with the letter A and ends with the letter Z.
story:
Charles sat at book club. There was a big rug with letters on it. Miss Poppy pointed at the letters one by one. "A," said Charles. "B," said Mia. "P!" said Charles. He clapped. "I said them all!"

Miss Poppy smiled. "P," she said. "But P is not the end." Charles frowned. His sock felt itchy. He wiggled his foot. "Is P the last letter?" he asked. "No," said Mia. "Sing with me and see."

They sang the letter song. "Q, R, S," sang Charles. More letters came after P! He tapped each one on the rug. He got to the last square. "Z!" he shouted. "Z is the end!" He laughed. The song had hidden letters, like an animal hiding in grass.

"Now tell me," said Miss Poppy. "Where does it start?" Charles pointed. "A!" he said. "A starts it. Z ends it." Then he dried his hands on his shirt and sang the whole song again, all the way from A to Z.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Soon means in a little while.
story:
Athena went to the store with Mama today. Yesterday Athena had seen pink balloons there. She wanted one so much. "Can we look now?" she asked. "Yes," said Mama. "We will buy bread first. Later we will look at balloons."

Athena put the bread in the cart. She put apples in the cart too. "Is it later now?" she asked. "Not yet," said Mama. "Soon, Athena. Soon means in a little while." Athena sighed. Waiting was hard.

Then Athena saw the bakery man put a cake in the window. His hands made the cake go round and round. The oven turned the cake big and gold. Athena watched. One thing made another thing happen. It was like magic, but real.

"Now it is later," said Mama. They walked to the balloon stand. Athena saw pink balloons, up high. "One for you," said Mama. Athena held the string. The balloon pulled her hand up, up, up.

"Tomorrow I will show it to Ben," said Athena. "Today it is mine." Outside, a big bus went by. The wind from the bus made her balloon dance. Athena laughed and held on tight. "Hello, balloon," she said. "We will go home now."

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: A number word always means the same amount: 'three' always means three things.
story:
Wyatt wanted grapes. "You can have three," said Mom. Wyatt looked at the bowl. The grapes were small.

He picked one, two, three small grapes. Then he saw a big grape. It was fat and round. "Maybe a big grape counts as two," he thought. He put the big grape in his hand too.

Mom shook her head with a smile. "Three is three," she said. Wyatt put one small grape back. One, two, three. The big grape stayed. A little bug crawled on the table. Wyatt watched it while he ate.

The big grape was sweet and cold. Juice ran down his chin. Mom gave him a napkin. "One, two, three," Wyatt said again. He counted his grapes, and every time, three meant three. "More please," he said.

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
knowledge_domain: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
fact: Spreading objects out or pushing them close together does not change how many there are.
story:
Oliver sat at the kitchen table. His big sister Poppy poured out buttons. "Let's count them!" said Oliver. "Yes!" said Poppy. She made two rows.

Oliver looked at the rows. One row went all the way across the table. The other row was bunched up in a small pile. "This one has more!" said Oliver. He pointed at the long row.

"Count them," said Poppy. Oliver touched each button in the long row. "One, two, three, four, five." Then he counted the small pile. "One, two, three, four, five."

Oliver jumped up. "Both rows have five!" He pushed the long row close together. He counted again. Still five! He spread the pile out wide. Still five!

Oliver laughed. His soft toy bee sat by the salt. He made the bee hop over both rows. "Five and five!" said the bee, in a funny little voice.

Oliver counted one more time, just to be sure. "Five!"

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: Stay where your grown-up can see you when you are out.
story:
Athena ran into the backyard. Her grandma sat on the step. The sun felt warm on Athena's arms.

"Stay where I can see you," said Grandma. Athena nodded. She stayed close to the step.

Then Athena saw something. A little train went by, far away, behind the tall fence. It looked so neat! Athena ran to the far end of the yard. She stood on her toes. But the fence was too tall. She could not see the train anymore.

Athena turned around. The fence was big. She could not see Grandma. Her tummy felt small and tight.

"Grandma?" she called. There was no answer. Athena ran back fast. Grandma was on the step. She was waving. Athena ran right into her arms. That felt better.

"You came back," said Grandma. "You stayed where I could see you."

Athena sat next to Grandma. They heard the train together. Choo, choo! Athena counted the cars. One, two, three.

They counted to ten. The sun went soft and warm. Athena stayed on the step. Grandma held her hand. That was the best place to be.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Seeds need water to start growing.
story:
Alexander dug a little hole in the dirt. He dropped in a seed and patted it flat. "Grow, little seed," he said.

Every morning he ran to the backyard swing. He swung high, then jumped off and looked at his garden. Nothing was there. Just dirt. Day after day, just dirt.

A bird landed nearby. It stuck out its tongue and chirped at the dry ground. Alexander touched the dirt. It was dry and crumbly, like crackers.

He ran inside. "Dad, my seeds will not grow!" he called.

Dad came out with the watering can. "Try this," he said. Alexander tipped it over the dirt. Water dripped down, dark and cool. He watered the spot every day after that.

One morning, something small and green stood in the dirt. It had two tiny leaves, new and soft. Alexander knelt down very close. "Hello," he whispered, and gave it a little more water.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
fact: A triangle has three sides and three corners.
story:
Ibrahim sat at the art table. He wanted to paint a house. He looked for a good shape. He found paper squares. He found paper circles too. Teacher Amna sat next to him. She had her brown spoon. She was mixing paint with it.

"Can a house be round?" Ibrahim asked. "No," he said. He put the circle aside. He picked up a square. He glued it down for the house walls. Then he looked for a roof. He held up a triangle. "How many corners does it have?" he asked. He touched each one. "One, two, three," he said. Three corners and three sides. The triangle sat on top of the square. The house had a roof.

Teacher Amna had her snack. Her sandwich was cut into triangles. Ibrahim pointed at a piece. "One, two, three," he said. Three corners again. She smiled and gave him a piece. He took a big bite.

Next to him, Sara dropped her brush. Paint was going to spill. "Teacher Amna!" Ibrahim yelled. She caught the cup with her brown spoon. Nothing spilled. Sara gave Ibrahim a paper rectangle. "For your door," she said. He glued it on. "One, two, three," he said, touching the roof corners one more time.

activity: going to the dentist for the first time
knowledge_domain: going to the dentist for the first time
fact: A dentist wears gloves when putting fingers or tools in your mouth.
story:
Harper sat in a big blue chair at the dentist. She held her gray mouse toy tight. "It will be okay, Mouse," she whispered. "One, two, three, we are brave."

A kind dentist walked in. His hands were blue. Harper stared. "Why are your hands blue?" she asked. "Do they hurt?"

The dentist smiled. "They are gloves," he said. He pinched one blue finger. Then he pulled it off. Under the glove, his hand was not blue at all.

"I wear the gloves when I put my fingers or my tools in your mouth," he said. "First I puts them on, then I looks inside."

Harper watched him snap on a new glove. The glove made a little pop sound. She giggled. "Say hi to my mouse first," she said. "He needs gloves too."

The dentist laughed softly. He held up one clean glove like a tiny blanket. He tucked it around the gray mouse. "All set," he said. "Open up, Harper. One, two, three."

Harper opened her mouth wide. Mouse watched from her lap, wearing his little blue blanket.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: After you sleep tonight and wake up, today will be called yesterday.
story: Henry put on his blue sweater. He ran to the park with Dad. The red truck was there. Henry wanted to ride it. But a girl was on it now. Henry had to wait. He felt a bit angry. He stomped his foot. Dad said, "We can come back tomorrow." Henry asked, "Where did today go?" Dad said, "After you sleep tonight, today will be called yesterday." Henry thought about that all day. At night he closed his eyes. He slept and slept. Then the sun came up. "It is today again!" said Henry. He ran to the park. The grass was wet. It had rained yesterday. The red truck sat all alone. Henry jumped on and rode round and round. "I waited, and now it is today!" he said. Dad clapped his hands.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
knowledge_domain: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
fact: Borrowed books have to be brought back to the library by a certain day, called the due date.
story:
Luna ran to the bookmobile. It was a little bus full of books. Dad held her hand.

"I want my own card," said Luna.

The librarian smiled. She made a card with Luna's name. "Pick one book," she said.

Luna picked a book about a red bird. She hugged it tight. "This book is mine forever!"

The librarian shook her head gently. "It has to come back on the due date," she said. "Then another kid can read it too."

Luna frowned. She did not want to move the book from her arms. The shelf looked empty where the red bird book had been.

"Will it be gone forever?" Luna asked.

"No," said Dad. "We bring it back. Then we can take it home again."

On the due day, Luna and Dad went back. Luna gave the librarian the book. She watched the librarian put it on the shelf. The empty spot was full again.

Luna picked it right up. "Hello, red bird," she said. "It's like a gift that comes back."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: During Diwali, many families light small clay oil lamps called diyas.
story:
It was Diwali night at Eleanor's house. Grandma called, "Come help with the diyas!"

Eleanor ran to the table. The diyas were small clay cups. Each one was cool to touch. They had no fire yet.

Eleanor counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four." She set them in a row. "Five, six, seven, eight." The row went all the way to the door.

"Are they ready?" Eleanor asked.

"Not yet," said Daddy. He had the matches. He lit one little wick. A tiny flame popped up. Then another, and another.

Eleanor clapped her hands. "The dark went away!"

The diyas glowed orange and gold. The oil inside smelled warm and a little messy on her fingers.

"More, more!" said Eleanor.

Daddy lit the last one. Eight little lamps, all in a line.

"Now it is Diwali," said Grandma. "Look how our night shines."

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: A cold can make your nose runny or stuffy.
story:
Victoria had a cold. She sat at the table with her oatmeal. Her nose felt funny. Sniff, sniff, went Victoria.

"You need a tissue," said Mom. "Your nose is runny." Mom put a tissue in Victoria's hand. Victoria wiped her nose. The tissue was wet. She had not known her nose could do that.

Victoria went back to her oatmeal. Sniff, sniff. The runny nose came back. "Tissue, please," said Victoria. Mom smiled and gave her one. Victoria held it ready all by herself. She hoped her nose would feel better soon.

After breakfast, they looked out the window. The sky was cloudy. They saw the big tree in the yard. Victoria sniffed one more time. Then she picked up her tissue. "I can do it myself," she said, and she wiped her own little nose.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: The word 'five' and the numeral 5 mean the same number.
story:
Axel sat down for dinner. He saw five carrots on his plate. "Wow!" said Axel.

Then he saw a big card by his plate. It had a 5 on it. "What is that?" he asked.

"That is the number five," said Dad.

Axel looked at the card. He looked at his carrots. He touched them one by one. "One, two, three, four, five," he said. He held up his fingers too. "One, two, three, four, five!"

Dad laughed. "Yes! Five carrots and the 5 card. The same."

"I want to count more!" said Axel. He asked Dad for more corn. Dad put some on his plate.

"One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight," said Axel. "Two more!"

Dad added two pieces. "Nine, ten!" said Axel. He clapped his hands.

Then Axel began to eat. He did not forget his carrots. "My tooth feels funny," he said. He pointed at a missing spot in his smile. "That tooth is missing!"

"Your big tooth will come," said Dad.

Axel grinned and took a big bite. "Ten bites!" he said. "One, two, three."

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
knowledge_domain: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
fact: Taking one object away from a group makes the number one smaller.
story:
Clara went to the community centre with her dad. The room had small tables and many toys. A big bell sat by the door. When it was time to start, a teacher rang the bell, and the children came to sit down. There was a boy there named Sam. He had a toy car in his hand.

The teacher put out two bowls of crackers. She asked, "Which bowl has more?" Clara pointed at the tall pile in the red bowl. The teacher said, "Let's count and see." Clara touched each cracker. "One, two, three, four, five." Then she counted the blue bowl. "One, two, three." The red bowl had more.

Clara wanted to eat a cracker. She took one from the red bowl. Then she counted again. "One, two, three, four." Now Sam counted the blue bowl. "One, two, three." Clara said, "Mine still has more!" Sam laughed. He took one from the blue bowl too. Clara counted his bowl. "One, two."

Sam pushed his toy car across the table. "Now you have more than me," he said. Clara slid two crackers to his bowl. She counted both bowls. "Four and four. The same!" Sam clapped his hands.

The teacher rang the bell again. It was time for juice. Clara held Sam's hand, and they walked to the little cups together. "You can sit by me," said Clara. Sam rolled his car along beside her, all the way to the snack table.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: In English, the words on a page are read from left to right.
story:
Emile found a thick red book on the rug. The cover had a rabbit and a little flag. He wanted to know the rabbit's name. He opened the book at the back. He put his finger on the last page. He slid it from the right side to the left side. The pictures jumped around all wrong.

Miss Ana sat down next to him. "Let me show you," she said. She turned the book around. "This is the front." She opened the front cover. Then she put her finger at the left side of the page. She slid it from left to right. "Bunny hops," she said. The words came out in a row.

"Can I try?" Emile asked. "Yes," said Miss Ana. Emile put his finger on the left. He slid it to the right. "Bunny hops to the flag," he said. He smiled and turned to the next page.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: A grown-up should check that bath water is warm, not hot, before you get in.
story:
Bennett ran into the backyard. He wanted to splash in his little pool today. He saw Mama filling it with the hose. The water looked warm and nice.

"Can I jump in now?" Bennett asked.

"Not yet," said Mama. She put her hand in the water. "A grown-up has to check. The water must be warm, not hot."

Bennett waited. He touched the tall fence. He saw light on the grass. He did a little dance.

Mama smiled. "The water is warm now. You can get in."

Bennett stepped in slowly. The water felt good on his toes. He stayed close to Mama and splashed with both hands. Water flew up and up.

"Again!" he said. "Do it again!"

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
knowledge_domain: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
fact: Borrowed books have to be brought back to the library by a certain day, called the due date.
story:
The bookmobile came to Luna's street. It was a little truck full of books. Luna held her mama's hand. The librarian smiled and said, "Today you get your very first library card." Luna took the card. It had her name on it.

Luna found a book about a red fire truck. She hugged it tight. "I want to keep it forever," she said. The librarian shook her head gently. "This book is borrowed," she said. "It has to come back by a certain day. That day is called the due date." Luna frowned. "Then it will be gone and the shelf will be empty."

"You can bring it back," said the librarian. "Then you can take a new one home." Luna thought about that. She moved the book in her arms and smiled. The librarian stamped a paper inside the book. Luna saw the mark. It showed the due date.

At home, Luna read the fire truck book three times. When the due day came, she and Mama walked to the bookmobile. Luna gave the book to the librarian. Then a boy took the fire truck book off the shelf. He hugged it, just like Luna had. Luna picked a book about the moon. "My new gift from the library," she said. The truck doors closed, and the bookmobile drove away. Luna waved until it turned the corner.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: A grown-up should check that bath water is warm, not hot, before you get in.
story:
Bennett ran into the backyard. His dog Buddy was splashing in the little pool. Bennett wanted to jump in too. But the hose had been lying in the sun. Mom held the hose and let water drip on her hand. "Too hot now," she said. "Let it run and cool." Bennett waited on the grass. He patted Buddy's soft ears.

The water ran onto the ground. Bennett put his hand under it. First it felt hot like soup. Then it felt warm like a blanket. Mom put her hand in too. "Now it is just right," she said. Bennett stepped in slowly. The water made his toes feel happy. Buddy shook and water flew everywhere.

"Can we do this again tomorrow?" Bennett asked. Mom laughed and turned off the hose. Bennett waved to the tall fence, where the light of the sun made the water shine. Buddy barked once, and Bennett barked back.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: Your nose has two openings called nostrils.
story:
Jules ran into the kitchen. Something smelled good. He used his nose to sniff. "Mama, what is that smell?" Mama was making pancakes. "Use your eyes to see," she said. Jules looked. Round pancakes sat on a plate.

Jules wanted to touch one. "Hot," said Mama. "You must wait." She put one pancake on a cool plate for him. Jules touched it with one finger. It was soft and warm. Mama poured batter into the pan. Jules heard it sizzle. Knock, knock. That was the door. "Daddy is home!" said Jules. He was not late after all.

Jules took a small bite. Yum, sweet! Then he wondered. How did his nose smell the pancakes? He ran to the hallway mirror. He looked at his face. There were two little openings in his nose. He breathed in. His nose moved a tiny bit. One opening, two openings. Both were working!

"How many openings does my nose have?" he asked Mama. He counted in the mirror. "One, two," he said. Mama laughed and put the top pancake on his plate. Jules sniffed it again. Both little openings took in the sweet smell. He took another big bite.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: Colors come in lighter and darker kinds, like light blue and dark blue, and both are still called blue.
story:
Snow fell past the window while Lucy played. "Look, a blue crayon," she said. Her brother Ben shook his head. "That one is too dark. That is not blue." Lucy held it up to her doll's dress. The dress was blue too, but a light blue, like the snow was almost white. "It is blue," said Lucy. "It is just dark blue."

"Let's ask the crayons," said Ben. They dumped them all out. Lucy picked the blue ones. "One, two, three, four, five!" She lined them up in a row. The first was very light. The last was very dark, deep as night. "They are all blue," said Lucy. "Light blue, dark blue, blue, blue, blue."

Ben tapped the darkest one. "Okay, it is blue. But it is sleepy blue." Lucy laughed. She drew a big deep blue sky. Then she added tiny white snow dots with her other hand.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Butter from the fridge is hard, and butter left out on the counter gets softer.
story:
Joshua ran into the school cooking classroom. Today he would make bread for his family! "I will stir the mix," he said. Teacher Mia smiled. Joshua counted the cups, one, two, three. He poured them in. He stirred and stirred. The mix looked like soft mud.

Next came the butter. Joshua opened the little fridge. He took out the butter. It was cold and hard. He pushed it with his spoon. The butter would not spread. It sat on the bread like a hard little rock. "Oh no," said Joshua. "My bread!"

Teacher Mia put the butter on the counter. "We will wait a bit," she said. Joshua waited. He tapped his spoon, one, two, three. Then he touched the butter. It felt soft now! He spread it on the warm bread. The butter went smooth and shiny. "Soft butter, happy bread, happy family!" Joshua carried the plate to the door. "Look what I made!"

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
fact: A big circle and a tiny circle are both circles, because size does not change a shape.
story:
Florence ran to the shape table at school. She wanted to make a sun for the class picture. The sun needed one big circle.

She found a big paper circle. Hooray! Then she wanted little circles for the sun's face. She found a tiny button on the craft tray.

Tom looked over. "That button can't be a circle," he said. "The clock on the wall is a circle. Your button is too small."

Florence held the button up high. She traced around it with her finger. Round and round it went. Then she looked at the clock. Round and round that went too.

"Watch this," she said. She pressed the button into the paint. She stamped it on her paper. A small circle appeared! She stamped it again and again.

"The big one is the sun," she said. "The little ones can be birds going to their nest." She stamped small circles across the sky.

Tom grabbed a button too. "I want to pay for my picture," he said, and he glued a button on like a coin. "A circle for money!"

Miss Patel hung both pictures on the safe wall by the window. Florence pointed at her sun. "Big circle, lots of little circles," she said. "They all go round!"

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
knowledge_domain: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
fact: Babies wear diapers because they cannot use the toilet yet.
story:
Bennett was at Grandma's house. A new baby sister was coming home soon. Bennett wanted to give her a gift.

"Let's make a picture," said Grandma. Bennett got his pencil. He drew a baby. He drew a cat. He drew a big red heart. Then he used the scissors to cut the paper. Grandma held the paper while he cut. The picture came out just right.

Next they went to the baby store. There were tiny socks and tiny hats. A boy there asked his mom, "Why so many diapers?" His mom said, "Babies wear diapers because they cannot use the toilet yet." Bennett listened. His baby sister would need lots of diapers. He counted them on the shelf. One, two, three, four, five. He put a big pack in the cart.

At last the baby came home. Bennett felt a little sad he could not play with her yet. But she grabbed his finger. Then she grabbed his picture too. Grandma put a fresh diaper on her. "Diaper, picture, baby," said Bennett. "All done." The baby yawned and fell asleep in Grandma's arms.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: Adding white paint to a color makes it lighter, so red with white becomes pink.
story:
Madeline went to the park with her dad. She wanted to paint a pink flower for Grandma's card. She had red, yellow, blue and green paint. But no pink paint at all.

First she looked around the park. She saw green grass. She saw a blue swing. She saw a yellow slide. She saw red flowers by the bench. "Red flowers are pretty," said Madeline. "But Grandma loves pink."

She sat at the picnic table. She opened her red paint. She dipped her brush. She painted a red flower on the card. "Too red," said Madeline. She wanted pink, pink, pink.

Then she saw a big bucket of white paint. Dad was painting the fence with it. Madeline had an idea. "Can I have a little white, please?" she asked. Dad helped her put one drop of white in her red paint. Madeline stirred it round and round, slowly, slowly. The red paint turned pink! "It's pink!" said Madeline. "White made my red light!"

She painted a pink flower for Grandma. She painted one pink petal, two pink petals, three pink petals. Then she ran to the high slide and slid down fast. Dad said, "Grandma will love it." Madeline held up her card and smiled. "Pink flower for Grandma!"

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: Eyelashes help keep dust and bits of dirt out of your eyes.
story: Anna was playing in the yard. The wind began to blow. Sand flew up in the air. Some sand got in Anna's eye. She blinked and blinked. "Ow," she said. The sand went away. Anna ran to Mama. "Why do my eyes blink at sand?" she asked. "Try and see," said Mama. Anna blinked again. She made it fast, then slow. Her little hairs on her eyelids moved too. "The sand lands on them," Anna said. "Then it falls off!" She put her hand near her eye. The soft little hairs tickled her finger. Anna heard the wind again. She smelled the flowers by the door. She touched the warm wall. The wind blew more sand. Anna blinked fast. Not one bit went in. "My eyelashes keep dust out of my eyes!" Anna said. She made a robot face. "Beep beep. My robot eyes are safe." Mama laughed. "Will the sand make you sad now?" she asked. "No," said Anna. "I cannot lose. I have eyelashes!" She ran back to play.

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
knowledge_domain: learning to swim at the local pool
fact: A lifeguard's job is to watch the swimmers and help anyone who needs it.
story:
Parker stood at the edge of the pool. The water was bright green and warm. His mom held his hand.

"Look up high," said Mom. Parker looked. A lady sat in a tall chair above the water. She wore a red suit and big sunglasses.

"Why is she up there?" Parker asked.

"She is the lifeguard," said Mom. "Her job is to watch the swimmers and help anyone who needs it."

Parker kicked his feet in the water. He held the wall. He let go for one second. Then he slipped. His arms went splash, splash.

The lifeguard blew her whistle. She pointed right at Parker. A pool helper came over fast and held him up.

"I saw you from up high," the lifeguard called down. "I can see everyone up here."

Parker looked up at her tall chair. From there she could see his mom, and the kids, and the whole pool.

Then it was time for lunch. Parker sat on a towel and ate cheese and crackers. After lunch, a green ball floated by. Parker tried to chase it along the edge. The lifeguard watched him the whole way.

"Nice walking, Parker," she said from up high. "I am still watching."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Written music uses marks called notes to show which sounds to play.
story:
Felix stood in the band room. He held a little drum. He wanted to play a song, but he did not know how.

Miss Kim had a big paper on the stand. Felix saw dots and lines on it. "What are the dots?" he asked.

Miss Kim smiled. "Those are notes," she said. "The notes show which sounds to play." She pointed. "Play here. Then here. Then here."

Felix hit the drum at each note. Boom. Boom. Boom. He waited between the notes. He tried again, slow and slow. The booms made a song!

A bird sat at the window. It cocked its head. Felix did not feel upset anymore. He played the song one more time, boom by boom. The bird stayed to listen.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In soccer, a team scores by getting the ball into the other team's goal.
story:
Juliette loved her soccer team. They played by the big pool. The grass was green and soft.

"Kick the ball to the goal," said Coach Ben. He pointed to the net far away. Juliette ran to the ball. She kicked it hard. But the ball went the wrong way! It rolled toward the tall net behind her.

"Oh no," said Juliette. The ball bumped into the net. The other team did not get a point. Coach Ben ran over. He turned Juliette around with kind hands. "Look this way," he said. "See that net? Kick there."

Juliette looked. The net was far away, by the pool fence. She got the ball again. She looked at the net first. Then she kicked. The ball rolled and rolled. It went into the net! "Goal!" her friends cheered.

Juliette clapped her hands. She kicked the ball the right way now. After the game, they would all stay for dinner by the pool. "I can kick to the net," Juliette told Coach Ben. He smiled and gave her a big thumbs up.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: A clock shows what time it is.
story:
Henry went to the park today. Yesterday it rained, so he could not go. "When can we play?" Henry asked. "Now," said Mom. Henry ran to the swings.

"Now we swing," said Henry. "Later we will get ice cream." But when was later? Henry asked again and again. Mom held up her phone. On it was a clock. "This clock shows what time it is," she said. The little hand pointed to a three. "When the hand moves to four, we go." Henry watched the hand. It did not move. He waited. He swung high. Then he looked again. The hand had moved! "It is four!" he shouted.

They got ice cream. Henry was not angry about waiting anymore. "Tomorrow," he asked, "can the clock say park time?" Mom laughed. "Yes. And tonight it will say bedtime." Henry licked his cone and waved goodbye to the swings.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: In English, there is a space between one word and the next.
story:
Margot sat on her bedroom floor. She wanted to write a note. It would say, "Come read to me, Grandpa." She held her crayon tight. She wrote and wrote. Then she ran to find Grandpa.

"Read my note!" said Margot. Grandpa looked and looked. He turned his head sideways. "Hmm," he said. "It says gobbledygook. Is it about a stinky sock?" Margot giggled. "No! It is not stinky! It says come read to me!" Grandpa shook his head. "All your letters are holding hands. One, two, three, four, all squished in a big hug."

So Margot went back to her note. She counted her words. One word: come. Two words: read. Three words: to. Four words: me. She left a little space after each word. "Words need a space between them," said Grandpa, peeking in. Margot added the spaces, one by one.

"Try now!" she said. Grandpa read it. "Come read to me, Grandpa!" he said out loud. "Why, yes! I will!" They sat on the bed. Grandpa opened the book at the front. He read page one. Then page two. Then page three. Margot snuggled close and said, "Now we sink into the pillows, too."

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
knowledge_domain: learning to swim at the local pool
fact: A lifeguard's job is to watch the swimmers and help anyone who needs it.
story:
Parker stood by the big blue pool. He wanted to swim like the big kids. Mom held his hand. "You can learn today," she said.

Parker looked up at the tall chair. A lifeguard sat up high. "Why does she sit way up there?" Parker asked. Mom said, "Watch and see."

Parker got in the shallow water. It was cool on his toes. He kicked and kicked. Then he saw a green ball float far away. He tried to chase it. His feet slipped. He went under for a moment.

Splash! The lifeguard blew her whistle. She pointed right at Parker. A helper came fast and lifted him up. "I saw you from up high," the lifeguard said. Parker held the helper's hand. From the tall chair, she could see everyone in the pool.

Parker kicked back to the steps. Mom hugged him. "Swim time is done for now," she said. "Lunch soon."

Parker looked up at the tall chair. He waved at the lifeguard. She waved back and kept watching the water.
